611.event_title: Dashrath Manjhi cuts a road through a hill by hand
611.event: Dashrath Manjhi, a poor labourer from the village of Gehlaur near Gaya, lived on one side of a rocky hill that forced villagers into a long detour to reach the nearest town and its services. After the death of his wife, he set out to cut a passage through the hill himself, working for about twenty-two years with a hammer and chisel. The finished cut, commonly described as about 360 feet long and 30 feet wide, greatly shortened the journey, and the Bihar government later honoured him as the Mountain Man.
611.explanation: A task that looked impossible for one man with hand tools was completed because he kept working at it year after year, alongside his ordinary labour.
611.tie_back: The kural says never to lose heart by calling a task too hard, because effort itself gives the strength to accomplish it, and Manjhi's road was cut by a man who simply refused to treat the hill as too big.
611._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural; reported dimensions and distances vary somewhat between sources, so the event field gives them only approximately.

612.event_title: Diderot carries the Encyclopedie through to completion after it is banned
612.event: Denis Diderot was co-editor of the Encyclopedie, whose first volume appeared in 1751. In 1758 his co-editor Jean le Rond d'Alembert withdrew, and in 1759 the royal privilege was revoked, the volumes already published were condemned, and the pope placed the work on the Index. Diderot nevertheless kept working, the last ten volumes of text were issued together in 1765, and the final volumes of plates appeared in 1772.
612.explanation: Abandoned by his partner and banned by the authorities at the halfway point, Diderot spent more than a decade finishing one of the defining works of the Enlightenment.
612.tie_back: The kural warns against letting effort slacken in the middle of a task, and Diderot, faced with every reason to stop halfway, carried the Encyclopedie through to its last volume.
612._accuracy_note: A very close fit for persisting through a task's crisis point; the kural's remark that the world abandons those who abandon work is implied rather than shown.

613.event_title: Tan Kah Kee builds a business empire and founds Xiamen University
613.event: Tan Kah Kee, a Chinese-born businessman in Singapore with little formal education, built a large business on pineapple canning, rice milling and above all rubber, which by the 1920s employed thousands of people. He used his fortune to found or support many schools in Singapore and China, including Nanyang Chinese High School in 1918. In 1921 he founded Xiamen University, the first university in China established by an overseas Chinese, and he funded it until 1937, when the government took it over.
613.explanation: Tan Kah Kee's generosity on this scale was possible only because of the fortune his years of hard work had produced, and he spent much of it on education.
613.tie_back: The kural says the proud distinction of helping others rests on hard work alone, and Tan Kah Kee's schools and university were built from the earnings of a lifetime of labour.
613._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of effort as the foundation of generosity; sources differ on the exact number of schools he helped found.

614.event_title: Robert Owen's cooperative community at New Harmony fails
614.event: In 1825 the British reformer Robert Owen bought the town of Harmony, Indiana, and invited people to join a cooperative community based on shared property and equality. The community attracted many intellectuals and many people with large families or few useful skills, and only a minority of its residents worked in productive trades such as farming, while plans for organising labour remained vague. By 1827 the experiment had failed, and Owen had lost most of his fortune.
614.explanation: Owen's generous vision of a community that would provide for all could not survive without enough organised, productive work to sustain it.
614.tie_back: The kural says generosity without the support of hard work fails like a sword in the hand of one who cannot use it, and New Harmony's noble aims collapsed for lack of the labour needed to pay for them.
614._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of good intentions undone by a lack of productive work; Owen himself was hardworking, and the community's failure also had causes in its governance and finances.

615.event_title: Maria Sklodowska works as a governess to pay for her sister's medical studies
615.place: Poland (then under Russian rule) and Paris, France
615.event: As a teenager in Warsaw, Maria Sklodowska, later Marie Curie, made a pact with her elder sister Bronya: Maria would work to support Bronya through medical school in Paris, and Bronya would later help pay for Maria's studies. Maria worked for several years as a governess and tutor, sending money to her sister while studying on her own in her spare time. In 1891 she went to Paris, lived at first in Bronya's home and enrolled at the Sorbonne.
615.explanation: By putting aside her own ambitions for years and working for her sister, the future double Nobel laureate became the support on which her family's hopes rested.
615.tie_back: The kural says one who prefers work to personal pleasure becomes a pillar who wipes away the troubles of kin and holds them up, and Maria's years as a governess held up her sister's future and then her own.
615._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of choosing work over one's own comfort to support family; sources differ slightly on her age when the arrangement began.

616.event_title: Konosuke Matsushita starts a workshop in his home in Osaka
616.event: On 7 March 1918, twenty-three-year-old Konosuke Matsushita founded Matsushita Electric Housewares Manufacturing Works in Osaka with his wife Mumeno and her younger brother Toshio Iue. Their first product was an improved attachment plug, made partly with metal parts recycled from used light bulbs, and sales were weak until Matsushita began dealing directly with wholesalers. The business was incorporated in 1935 as Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. and became one of the world's largest electronics makers, renamed Panasonic in 2008.
616.explanation: A three-person family workshop grew, through persistent effort, into a global company and a source of prosperity for many thousands of employees.
616.tie_back: The kural says effort builds up prosperity while lack of effort ushers in poverty, and the Matsushita workshop is a classic case of wealth built from almost nothing by work.
616._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of effort creating prosperity; the kural's contrasting half, idleness bringing poverty, is not shown.

617.event_title: Alexander Fleming notices the mould that leads to penicillin
617.place: St Mary's Hospital, London, United Kingdom
617.event: Returning from holiday on 3 September 1928, the bacteriologist Alexander Fleming began sorting through culture plates of Staphylococcus bacteria in his laboratory. On one plate contaminated by a mould he saw that the bacteria around the mould had been destroyed, and he went on to show that the mould produced a substance, which he named penicillin, that killed many kinds of bacteria. He published his findings in 1929, and penicillin was later developed into a medicine by Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their Oxford team; the three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.
617.explanation: A chance contamination became a medical revolution only because an experienced researcher was at work, paying attention, and followed up what he saw.
617.tie_back: The kural says good fortune dwells in the effort of the industrious, and Fleming's lucky mould brought its fortune to the world through a working scientist who was ready to recognise it.
617._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of fortune favouring the diligent; the kural's contrasting image of misfortune dwelling with the lazy has no counterpart here.

618.event_title: Frida Kahlo teaches herself to paint after her bus accident
618.event: On 17 September 1925, eighteen-year-old Frida Kahlo was severely injured when the bus she was riding in was struck by a streetcar in Mexico City, and she spent months in plaster casts, largely confined to bed. Her mother had a special easel made so she could paint lying down, and a mirror was fixed above her bed so she could study her own face. Teaching herself, she produced her first known work, Self-Portrait Wearing a Velvet Dress, in 1926, and went on to become one of the most celebrated painters of the twentieth century.
618.explanation: Kahlo did not choose her injuries, which affected her for the rest of her life, but she chose to work within their limits, and that work made her name.
618.tie_back: The kural says misfortune is no disgrace, only the failure to make an effort is, and Kahlo's accident brought no shame on her while the effort she made from her bed brought lasting honour.
618._accuracy_note: A strong fit, especially under the commentators' reading of the kural as saying that physical disability is no disgrace while lack of effort is.

619.event_title: Dorando Pietri is disqualified from the Olympic marathon and honoured by the Queen
619.event: In the marathon at the 1908 London Olympic Games, the Italian runner Dorando Pietri entered the stadium first but, exhausted, collapsed several times and went the wrong way, and officials helped him across the finish line. He was disqualified for receiving outside assistance, and the gold medal went to the American Johnny Hayes. The next day Queen Alexandra presented Pietri with a special silver-gilt cup, and his effort made him a popular hero.
619.explanation: Pietri was denied the victory he had all but reached, yet his extraordinary effort earned a unique royal honour and lasting fame.
619.tie_back: The kural says that even when fate keeps the goal out of reach, effort still pays the wages of one's toil, and Pietri lost the gold but received a reward of his own for what his body had endured.
619._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: the goal was lost through circumstance while the effort itself was rewarded.

620.event_title: Lis Hartel wins an Olympic dressage medal after polio
620.event: In 1944 the Danish rider Lis Hartel, then twenty-three and pregnant, contracted polio and was left paralysed below the knees. After years of rehabilitation she returned to competition, finishing second at the 1947 Scandinavian championships, and at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics, the first Games at which women could compete against men in dressage, she won the silver medal on her horse Jubilee. She needed help to mount and dismount, and the gold medallist Henri Saint Cyr helped her onto the podium; she won silver again in 1956.
620.explanation: A rider whom illness seemed to have shut out of her sport became the first woman to win an Olympic equestrian medal.
620.tie_back: The kural says those who strive without faltering or slackening will see even fate turn its back, and Hartel's unbroken effort carried her past what polio seemed to have decided for her.
620._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of effort overcoming an apparently fixed fate; her paralysis remained, so fate was overcome in its effects rather than reversed.
